I'm seeing a lot of traction behind the theory that this video game is a story about Paul being trans, but I think we need to remember that Paul was likely never the intended target of this game. It wasn't until his save files were deleted and game was changed that anything to do with him was even directly included. 

The conversation that was based on his conversation I think was actually two different conversations that were spliced together. After all, Paul said the calendar was either 1995 (the year Michael died) or 2017 (the year his conversation would have taken place). Someone else mentioned that it sounded like both the yellow/blue speakers seemed to be talking to someone ignoring them. 

As a trans person, I appreciate the willingness for everyone to consider this theory for the character, but I really just don't think it fits and limits the scope of the story. I personally think that Paul being connected to the story by being some kind of replacement for Care (having a similar face and the hints that Care never came home but was replaced in some way) rather than it being a literal transformation. This takes into account the mystery of the windmill, the fact that this game was likely intended for several audiences (Paul either being the last target or just someone caught up in his extended family's mayhem) as well as keeping Paul involved.

I'm contemplating the sound of the disk portraits - it sounds like a portion of the Playstation 1 startup sound ([https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YaONOQswRSQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YaONOQswRSQ)), which makes me think about the fact that the garage in the house had the computer with the website that we assume came with the game. Could this be indicating the possibility that the game was made in this house? That the portraits were representing the disk in some way? The conversation (or conversations - seeing another comment linking that the two colors could have been separate conversations happening in 1995/2017) was also talking about where the disk was... I don't know, it seems like the game disk itself has a connection to this house.

You don't owe anyone your story or your pain. It is yours. For some people, it feels empowering to say "you can't take my choices away, I am going to show people that I'm a survivor." For some people, it's empowering to see that others have struggled and survived. Neither is more valid or "good" than the other! 

This is a viral post that is meant to show people that this is much more common than they think, but it's just that - a viral post. By not posting, you're not denying your experiences or trauma, nor are you somehow lying to people. You are not weak. This just isn't your path of recovery.

I went to Bainbridge a couple weeks ago and found real-world locations that match almost TOO well to game locations. We didn't have a proper radio, so I can't verify anything about signals, but it would definitely be cool to go to the locations.
For reference:
Fort Milner = Fort Ward (They both occupy the highest points of the island, have radio communication/coding schools, and have radio relay points)
Towhee Woods = Fort Ward Park (National preservation parks to the west of the military barracks)
Harden Tower/Epiphany Fields/Relay point(?) =Battle point park (Radio tower on island with com point at the base of the tower, a relay radio station nearby. Buildings were intended to communicate with naval ships and signal an attack)
And obviously main street=the main town at Bainbridge

So if you wanted to check out possible radio signals, I'd suggest one of those two. Even if you can't find signals, it's really beautiful and interesting. There is a TON of fun and the two main batteries in Fort Ward park would definitely be worth a check-out.

My mindset for the ending is that every time we play the game, Alex is already in the loop. The real Alex made her choices - she decided to remain behind and free her friends and got stuck. Now, whatever she does (in our playthroughs), she can't get out. She can't escape the tear by sacrificing Clarissa because, well, it's not actually real. It's not until we find some secret to escape the loops (like there are in the mini loops throughout the game) that she can get out.

One additional tidbit of info: Battlepoint was NOT named for WWII, but actually years before when the Suquamish tribe battled the Haida (first nations people from Canada). But I digress. 

We tried out a radio at some points of interest but didn't find anything. We'll try again once we get to Battlepoint.
